newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan hopeful Israel will lift trade barriers.
newsitem.headline: Jordan hopeful Israel will lift trade barriers.

text.p: Jordanian officials said on Wednesday Israel had agreed in principle to new steps to lift trade barriers with Israel and the West Bank and boost the flow of goods.

Minister of Industry and Trade Ali Abu Al-Ragheb said talks with his Israeli counterpart Natan Sharansky in Israel on Wednesday would review a 1995 trade protocol to expand customs exemptions on lists of Jordanian goods and allow better access to its industry to the much coveted Palestinian markets.
"There are good expectations that we will get...more exemptions on the list of goods and a new arrangement for transporting goods to the Palestinian Authority," Abu Al-Ragheb told Reuters.

Officials also said Jordan secured over the last few days an Israeli pledge to allow "door-to-door" delivery of Jordanian goods to Israel, and to apply a similiar arrangement for Palestinian imports of cement and oil and petroleum products refined in Jordan.
Exports now have to go through a costly and cumberscome "back-to back" system -- taking goods off Jordanian trucks on one side of the border and loading them on Israeli trucks on the other.

Jordanians say the system, which Israel says is dictated by security needs, is protectionism in disguise to keep Jordanian goods uncompetitive in the Israeli market and keep a $2 billion Palestinian market captive for Israel.

Jordan's Transport Minister Nasser al-Lawzi told Reuters the new trucking accord will lead to a big reduction in cost and time of transport that will raise exports to both Israel and the Palestinian areas.
Officials blame the back-to-back system and tough Israeli security measures for the limited bilateral trade since a long delayed cross-border trade accord came into effect in June.

Officials will also press in the talks on Wednesday for wider customs exemption with Israel on the grounds that a three-tier preferential treatment system granted under last year's trade accord were not sufficient.

Jordan and Israel signed last year a trade agreement that included a list of Jordanian products that were granted preferential treatment over goods from other countries on three levels: tax free, 20 or 50 percent reductions in customs.
A limited list of Israeli goods got reductions of 10 percent. The uneven tariff reductions were in recognition of the different sizes of the economy.
But businessmen such as Omar Salah, an leading industrialist keen to break into the Israeli market, say additional duties Israel imposes has made Jordanian products uncompetitive.
Jordanian officials say this has led to a trade deficit with Israel since the trade accord came into effect despite the price competiteveness of products.

Jordan is wary of the vastly larger Israeli economy and says it must assess the impact of trade with Israel on its industry before discussing free trade arrangements. It hopes it can address that by a widening of customs exemptions.
